Group A has test scores {8, 12, 14, 16} (average 12.5). Group B has test scores {2, 4, 6} (average 4). Move the score of 8 from Group A to Group B — no individual score changes value, it just switches groups. What happens to the average of EACH group?
choices: Both averages stay exactly the same, since no individual score's value changed
Both averages go down, because moving any single element always increases the variance of both groups
Group A's average goes up but Group B's average goes down, since B just gained a comparatively low score
Both averages go up (A: 12.5 to 14, B: 4 to 5) — a value that's below the mean of the group it leaves but above the mean of the group it joins raises both

questions.q: In the general population, being funny and being talented are completely independent traits. A talent show accepts anyone who is funny OR talented (or both), rejecting only people who are neither. Among the accepted contestants, are being funny and being talented now positively correlated, negatively correlated, or still independent?
choices: Positively correlated — accepted contestants who are funny are more likely to also be talented
Still independent — a selection filter cannot create a correlation that wasn't present in the underlying population
It depends on the exact numbers and cannot be determined in general
Negatively correlated — funny accepted contestants are less likely to also be talented than non-funny accepted contestants are, purely because of how the OR-filter selects people

questions.q: A bus route has a repeating cycle of gaps between arrivals: 2, 2, 2, then 18 minutes, then it repeats. The average gap between buses is (2+2+2+18)/4 = 6 minutes. If you walk up to the stop at a uniformly random moment in time, what is your EXPECTED waiting time until the next bus?
choices: 1.5 minutes, since three of the four gaps are only 2 minutes long
7 minutes — you're disproportionately likely to arrive during the long 18-minute gap, which pulls the expectation above 'half the average'
6 minutes — the length of one full average gap
3 minutes — half the average gap, as you'd normally expect

questions.q: Two hospitals treat kidney stones with Treatment A and Treatment B. For small stones: A succeeds in 81 of 87 cases; B succeeds in 234 of 270 cases. For large stones: A succeeds in 192 of 263 cases; B succeeds in 55 of 80 cases. Treatment A has the higher success rate in BOTH the small-stone group and the large-stone group. Which treatment has the higher success rate when all 350 patients treated with each method are combined?
choices: It cannot be determined without knowing individual patient outcomes
Treatment A — since it wins in both subgroups, it must win overall
Treatment B — because it treated a much higher share of the easier small-stone cases, which pulls its combined average above A's

questions.q: In a small social network of 5 people, X is friends with A, B, C, and D, and none of A, B, C, D are friends with each other. So X has 4 friends, while A, B, C, and D each have exactly 1 friend. If you compute, for every person, the average number of friends THEIR friends have, and then average that across all 5 people, how does that population-wide figure compare to the network's actual average number of friends per person (1.6)?
choices: Lower than 1.6, since X already has the most friends and X's own friends can't also be unusually popular
It's only higher because this particular network happens to have an odd number of people
Exactly 1.6, since any such average must equal the population's raw average
Higher than 1.6 — specifically 3.4, since the highly-connected person X is listed as 'a friend' by four different people, so their high friend-count gets counted four times over
